intro: The New Testament is short. Its 27 books fit in the back quarter of most Bibles. Yet they were written across a huge world, from Jerusalem to Rome, in a time of Roman rule, Jewish debate and long sea voyages. This unit reads those books inside that world. It asks who ruled, who argued, who traveled and who wrote.

You will read the four Gospels as four portraits of one teacher, alike and different. You will follow the book of Acts from a Jerusalem festival to a Roman prison. You will read letters as letters, with senders, receivers and reasons. You will open Revelation and learn how an apocalypse works. And you will trace how these books, and not others, became a canon.

Throughout, the course describes and attributes. It says what the text says and what Christians, Jews, Muslims and scholars have made of it. It does not say who is right. By the end you will be able to name each kind of writing, place it in its time, and explain how two readers can read the same page differently.
bigQuestion: How does knowing the Roman and Jewish world of the first century change the way you read the New Testament?

write.prompt: How does a New Testament writer use the shape of a genre to make a point? Choose either a Gospel scene (for example Matthew 22:15–22 or Luke 10:25–37), a letter (Philemon 1–25 or 1 Corinthians 13), or a vision (Revelation 21:1–4). Cite two or three passages by book, chapter and verse. Explain what the text says, how its genre works, and how at least two kinds of readers have read it.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse every time you cite the text.

title: The New Testament in Its World

chapters.title: Gospels: Four Portraits, One Roman World
chapters.bigQuestion: How do four different Gospels, written in a Roman world, tell the story of one teacher from Galilee?

story.title: A Coin and a Trap
story.kicker: In the Temple courts, a small silver coin becomes the center of a question meant to catch a teacher out.
paragraphs: Matthew 22 tells of a day in Jerusalem, in the courts of the Temple. Jesus is teaching. A group walks up with a question. Some are Pharisees, teachers of the law. Others, the text says, are supporters of Herod, the family Rome let rule. They do not agree on much. But today they have one plan.

Their question sounds polite. Is it right, they ask, to pay the tax to Caesar, or not? The trap is in the two answers. Say yes, and the crowd hears a teacher taking Rome's side. Say no, and the Romans hear a rebel. Either way, the questioners win.

Jesus asks to see the coin used for the tax. Someone hands him a denarius. On it is the face of the emperor and his title. Whose picture is this, he asks, and whose name? Caesar's, they answer. Then give Caesar what is Caesar's, he says, and give God what is God's.

The Gospel says the questioners were amazed, and they walked away. Readers have argued for two thousand years about what the answer means. But the scene shows something else too. It shows a world. There is a Temple, a Roman tax, a coin with an emperor's face, and groups who disagree about how to live under Rome.

This chapter reads the four Gospels inside that world. We will meet the rulers, the groups and the places. We will ask when each Gospel was written, and why they are alike and different. And we will read the stories closely, as literature and history, the way a class in a public school can.
story.think: Why would a question about a tax be dangerous to answer in Jerusalem under Roman rule?

lessons.title: Rome, Herod and Pilate
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels are set in a land ruled by Rome through local kings and Roman governors.
reading: The Gospels tell their stories in a small corner of the Roman Empire. Rome took control of the region in 63 BCE. It ruled through local kings at first. The best known is *Herod* the Great, a king who rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem on a grand scale. Matthew 2 sets the birth of Jesus in his reign. Herod died c. 4 BCE, and Rome split his kingdom among his sons.

Galilee, in the north, went to Herod Antipas. Luke 3 names him as ruler when John the Baptist begins to preach. Judea, in the south, soon came under a Roman governor instead. The governor in the Gospels is Pontius *Pilate*. He held office c. 26 to 36 CE. All four Gospels say Pilate ordered the death of Jesus. Rome, not local rulers, held the power to execute.

Roman rule meant taxes, soldiers and coins with the emperor's face. It also meant a *census*, a count of people for taxing. Luke 2 opens the birth story with a census. Historians debate the date and details of that census. What is clear is that the Gospels expect readers to know this world. A tax collector, a centurion and a governor all appear as ordinary parts of the scene.

In 1961 archaeologists at Caesarea found a stone with Pilate's name and title on it. It is the first object outside written texts to name him. Finds like this do not prove or disprove what the Gospels say about him. They show that the setting is a real place and time that can be studied.

words.d: the family Rome let rule parts of the land; Herod the Great rebuilt the Temple and died c. 4 BCE
Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea c. 26–36 CE, who the Gospels say ordered the death of Jesus
an official count of people, often for taxes; Luke 2 begins the birth story with one

look.title: Rulers in the Gospel World
rows: Rome takes control of the region (BCE)
look.cite: Commonly cited dates from Josephus's histories and modern surveys of the period; some are approximate
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Herod's death and the Temple's destruction?

check.q: Who does every Gospel name as the Roman governor who ordered the death of Jesus?
check.why: All four Gospels place the sentence with Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea; Rome held the power to execute.

check.q: Which Gospel opens its birth story with a Roman census?
check.why: Luke 2 begins with a census ordered by the emperor; Mark and John have no birth story, and Acts is not a Gospel.

check.q: What did the stone found at Caesarea in 1961 show?
choices: That the census took place in 6 CE
That Pilate was a real official with that title
That Jesus was born in Bethlehem
check.why: The stone carries Pilate's name and title; it confirms the man and his office, not the events of the Gospels.

lessons.title: The Temple and the Groups
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish life in the Gospels centered on the Temple, and several groups disagreed about how to keep the Torah under Rome.
reading: The Temple in Jerusalem was the center of Jewish worship in the time of the Gospels. Priests offered sacrifices there. Pilgrims came for festivals like Passover. Herod's rebuilding made it one of the largest sacred sites in the Roman world. The Gospels return to it again and again. Jesus teaches in its courts and, in a famous scene, overturns the tables of the money changers.

Within Jewish life, groups differed about how to live faithfully. The *Pharisees* were teachers who applied the Torah to daily life. They believed in resurrection and in oral traditions passed down from teacher to student. Many scholars see them as the ancestors of later rabbinic Judaism. The Gospels show Jesus often arguing with Pharisees, but also eating with them and sharing many of their views.

The *Sadducees* were linked to the priests and the Temple. The Gospels say they did not believe in resurrection. The historian Josephus describes them as a small group with influence among the wealthy. A third group, the *Essenes*, lived apart, some in a community by the Dead Sea. The Gospels never name them. A fourth kind of people, whom Josephus and the Gospels call *Zealots*, wanted to resist Rome by force.

Reading the Gospels well means keeping these groups straight. It also means care. Christian readers have sometimes turned "Pharisee" into an insult. Jewish readers point out that the Pharisees were careful, serious teachers. A fair reading names each group by what it taught, not by a verdict.

words.d: Jewish teachers who applied the Torah to daily life and believed in resurrection; ancestors of later rabbinic Judaism, many scholars say
a group tied to the priests and the Temple; the Gospels say they did not believe in resurrection
a Jewish group that lived apart, some in a community near the Dead Sea; not named in the Gospels
people who wanted to resist Roman rule by force; one of Jesus's followers is called Simon the Zealot

look.title: Four Groups, One Question
look.text: Imagine the same question put to four people in Jerusalem around 30 CE: 'How should we live under Rome?' A Pharisee says, keep the Torah carefully in every part of daily life. A Sadducee says, keep the Temple and its sacrifices running. An Essene says, leave the city and live pure in the desert. A Zealot says, fight.
look.prompt: Which of these four answers does the Gospels' Jesus sound closest to, and which farthest? Use a passage to back up your view.

check.q: Which group did the Gospels say did NOT believe in resurrection?
check.why: The Gospels and Josephus both say the Sadducees, tied to the Temple priests, rejected resurrection; the Pharisees accepted it.

check.q: Which group is never named in the Gospels?
check.why: The Essenes are known from Josephus and, many scholars think, from the Dead Sea Scrolls, but the Gospels never mention them.

check.q: Many scholars see which group as the ancestors of later rabbinic Judaism?
check.why: The Pharisees' focus on Torah in daily life and on oral tradition carried on into rabbinic Judaism after the Temple fell.

lessons.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
lessons.mainIdea: Scrolls found near the Dead Sea in 1947 give a rare window into Jewish life and scripture in the time of the Gospels.
reading: In 1947 a shepherd near the Dead Sea threw a stone into a cave and heard pottery break. Inside were jars holding old scrolls. Over the next years, searchers found more caves near a site called *Qumran*. Together the finds are called the Dead Sea *Scrolls*. They hold about 900 manuscripts, most in pieces, written mainly in Hebrew and Aramaic.

The scrolls date from about 250 BCE to 70 CE. That is the world just before and during the time of the Gospels. About a quarter of them are copies of books of the Hebrew Bible. Every book except Esther is present. Before 1947, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts were from around 1000 CE. The scrolls pushed the evidence back a thousand years.

Other scrolls belong to the community itself. They include rules for shared life, hymns, and commentaries on the prophets. Many scholars think the community was Essene, though not all agree. The scrolls never mention Jesus or the early Christians. Their value for Gospel study is the setting. They show how some Jews of that time read scripture, waited for God to act, and shared meals and property.

Studying the scrolls is a good example of careful reading. Scholars compare a scroll of Isaiah with later copies and note the differences. They date the ink and the handwriting. They ask what the text says before asking what it means. That is the same method this course uses for the Gospels.

words.d: the site near the Dead Sea where the scrolls were found in caves, starting in 1947
the Dead Sea Scrolls, about 900 manuscripts from c. 250 BCE to 70 CE, including the oldest known copies of Hebrew Bible books
a text written by hand; before printing, every copy of a book was one

look.title: What the Scrolls Hold
look.cite: Rounded figures commonly cited in introductions to the Dead Sea Scrolls; counts differ by how fragments are grouped
look.prompt: Which biblical books seem to have been copied most at Qumran, and what might that suggest about what the community read?

check.q: What are the Dead Sea Scrolls?
choices: Greek copies of the four Gospels
Ancient Jewish manuscripts found in caves near Qumran
check.why: The scrolls are Hebrew and Aramaic manuscripts from c. 250 BCE to 70 CE, found in caves near the Dead Sea starting in 1947.

check.q: Which book of the Hebrew Bible is missing from the scrolls?
check.why: Every Hebrew Bible book has been found except Esther; Isaiah, Psalms and Deuteronomy appear in many copies.

check.q: How do the scrolls help readers of the Gospels?
choices: They show the Jewish world and reading habits of the time
They contain the earliest copy of Mark
They prove the Gospels are accurate
check.why: The scrolls never mention Jesus; their value is the setting they reveal, not a verdict on the Gospels.

lessons.title: What a Gospel Is
lessons.mainIdea: A gospel is an ancient kind of life-story written to persuade, and the New Testament has four of them.
reading: The word *gospel* comes from an Old English word meaning "good news." It translates the Greek word euangelion. Mark 1:1 opens with it: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ. At first the word meant the message itself. Later it became the name for the four books that tell the story of Jesus: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.

A gospel is a genre, a kind of writing. It looks most like an ancient *biography*, a life of a famous person. Greek and Roman writers produced many of these. But the Gospels have a purpose beyond information. John 20:31 says its stories were written so that readers may believe. The Gospels tell a life to persuade, and they say so.

That shapes how a careful reader works. A gospel is not a modern news report. It chooses scenes, orders them, and repeats themes. Each writer, whom tradition names an *evangelist*, has a point of view. Reading a gospel well means asking what each writer includes, leaves out and emphasizes. Christians read the Gospels as scripture. Scholars also read them as ancient texts with authors and audiences. A public-school class can do the second while respecting the first.

words.d: "good news"; the message about Jesus, and the name of the four books that tell his story
a written life of a person; ancient biographies chose scenes to show a person's character
the traditional name for a Gospel writer: Matthew, Mark, Luke or John

look.title: How Mark Begins
look.text: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God;
look.prompt: Mark opens with no birth story and no family tree. What does this first line tell you the book is about and how it will read?

check.q: What does the word "gospel" mean?
check.why: Gospel translates the Greek euangelion, "good news"; it named the message first and the four books later.

check.q: Which ancient genre do the Gospels most resemble?
check.why: Ancient lives of famous people chose scenes to show character; the Gospels work the same way, with a stated purpose.

check.q: According to John 20:31, why was that Gospel written?
choices: To record every event in order
check.why: John states its purpose openly: the stories are chosen so that readers may believe.

lessons.title: When the Gospels Were Written
lessons.mainIdea: Most scholars date the Gospels to c. 65–100 CE, with Mark first and John last.
reading: None of the Gospels names its author inside the text. The names Matthew, Mark, Luke and John come from early Christian tradition, attached by the second century. Scholars date the books by clues inside them and by when other writers first quote them. Most place all four between about 65 and 100 CE. That is one to three generations after the events they describe.

Most scholars think *Mark* came first, around 65 to 75 CE. Mark 13 seems to know the war with Rome that ended with the Temple's destruction in 70 CE. Matthew and Luke are usually dated c. 80 to 90 CE. Both appear to use Mark as a source. John is usually placed c. 90 to 100 CE. Its style and stories differ from the other three.

Some scholars argue for earlier dates, and some for later. The dates are estimates, so this course writes "c." before them. What matters for a reader is the order and the gap. The Gospels were written in Greek, decades after Jesus, for communities across the Roman world. Before that, stories about Jesus were passed on by word of mouth, what scholars call *oral tradition*.

Christians hold different views about what this means. Some stress that the writers relied on eyewitnesses. Others stress the freedom each writer took. A class does not have to settle that. It can note the evidence, hold the dates loosely and read each book on its own terms.

words.d: the shortest Gospel and, most scholars think, the first, written c. 65–75 CE
stories and sayings passed on by speaking before they were written down

look.title: Dates Most Scholars Give the Gospels
look.cite: Common scholarly ranges as summarized in standard New Testament introductions; dates are debated
look.prompt: If Jesus's public teaching is usually placed around 30 CE, how long a gap separates it from the earliest Gospel? What might change in that time?

check.q: Which Gospel do most scholars think was written first?
check.why: Mark is usually dated c. 65–75 CE, and Matthew and Luke seem to use it as a source.

check.q: In what language were the Gospels written?
check.why: All four Gospels were written in Greek, the common language of the eastern Roman Empire; Jesus likely spoke Aramaic.

check.q: Why does this course put "c." before Gospel dates?
choices: Because the Gospels give the dates themselves
Because the dates are in Roman years
Because the dates are scholarly estimates, not certain
Because the Gospels were written in Rome
check.why: No Gospel dates itself; scholars estimate from clues in the text, so the dates are approximate.

lessons.title: The Synoptics and John
lessons.mainIdea: Matthew, Mark and Luke share so much that they are called the Synoptics; John tells the story its own way.
reading: Lay Matthew, Mark and Luke side by side and a pattern appears. They share many of the same stories, often in the same order and with the same words. Because they can be "seen together," they are called the *Synoptic* Gospels. Most scholars explain the likeness by saying Matthew and Luke both used Mark. Many also think they shared a second source of sayings, which scholars call *Q*. Not everyone agrees on Q.

John is different. It has no parables of the familiar kind and no birth story. It has long speeches and a few great signs, like turning water into wine. Jesus in John speaks openly of who he is, using phrases like "I am the bread of life." John also tells of several trips to Jerusalem, where the Synoptics tell of one. Most scholars think John was written last and knew the Synoptic tradition, but wrote independently.

Christians have read the four together for a long time. In the second century some tried to merge them into one story. The church kept four instead. Readers have compared them to four portraits of one person, each from a different angle. A careful reader in a public school does the same thing. Notice what each Gospel shares, and notice where each stands alone.

words.d: "seen together"; Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share many stories, order and wording
a source of sayings that many scholars think Matthew and Luke both used; no copy has been found

look.title: One Story, Three Tellings
look.text: Mark 1 says Jesus was baptized by John in the Jordan, and a voice from heaven spoke to him: 'Thou art my beloved Son.' Matthew 3 tells the same scene, but the voice speaks to the crowd: 'This is my beloved Son.' Luke 3 says Jesus was praying when the heavens opened. John 1 does not describe the baptism at all; John the Baptist reports what he saw.
look.prompt: List one thing all four accounts share and one thing each changes. What might each change show about the writer's aim?

check.q: Which three Gospels are called the Synoptics?
check.why: Matthew, Mark and Luke share stories, order and wording, so they can be "seen together"; John stands apart.

check.q: What is "Q" in Gospel study?
choices: A sayings source many scholars think Matthew and Luke shared
A Roman record of Jesus's trial
check.why: Q is a proposed written collection of sayings; it explains material Matthew and Luke share that is not in Mark.

check.q: Which feature belongs to John and not to the Synoptics?
choices: Long speeches in which Jesus says "I am"
check.why: John's Jesus speaks in long discourses with "I am" sayings; the Synoptics have parables and one final journey to Jerusalem.

lessons.title: Parables Close Up
lessons.mainIdea: A parable is a short story that makes the listener think, and the Gospels record dozens of them.
reading: A *parable* is a short story drawn from daily life that carries a point about something bigger. Jesus in the Synoptics teaches in parables about seeds, sheep, coins, workers and feasts. Mark 4 says he taught the crowds this way. Jewish teachers of the same era also used short stories, called meshalim in Hebrew, so parables would have been a familiar form.

Take the sower in Mark 4. A farmer scatters seed. Some falls on the path, some on rock, some among thorns, some on good soil. Only the last grows. The story ends, and the listener is left to work out what the seed and the soils mean. Mark then adds an explanation given to the disciples in private. Many scholars think that layering shows how the early church used the story.

Parables often surprise. In Luke 10 a man is robbed and left on the road. A priest and a Levite pass by. The one who stops is a *Samaritan*, a member of a group that Jews of Judea and Galilee often distrusted. The story turns the listener's expectation over. Jesus ends by asking which of the three was a neighbor. The lawyer who asked cannot even say the word Samaritan. He says, the one who showed mercy.

Readers have taken parables many ways. Some early Christians read every detail as a symbol. Many modern scholars read each parable for its one sharp point. Either way, the form invites the reader to do the work. That is why a class can discuss a parable without being told what to believe.

words.d: a short story from daily life that carries a bigger point and makes the listener think
a member of a group living between Judea and Galilee, often distrusted by their neighbors; the hero of Luke 10's parable

look.title: The End of the Good Samaritan
look.text: Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves? And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
look.prompt: The lawyer asked, "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus's closing question changes the wording. How, and why might that matter?

check.q: What is a parable?
choices: A list of rules for the disciples
A prayer said in the Temple
A short story from daily life with a bigger point
A vision of the end of the world
check.why: Parables use seeds, sheep, coins and travelers to carry a point the listener must work out.

check.q: In the parable of the sower, which seed grows?
check.why: Mark 4 says only the seed on good soil grows; the other three are lost to birds, sun and thorns.

check.q: Why does the Samaritan surprise the listener in Luke 10?
choices: Samaritans were often distrusted, yet he is the one who helps
Samaritans were priests, so his help was expected
He was the man who was robbed
He was one of the twelve disciples
check.why: The story makes the hero a member of a distrusted group, after a priest and a Levite pass by.

lessons.title: The Sermon on the Mount
lessons.mainIdea: Matthew 5–7 gathers Jesus's teaching into one long sermon that opens with blessings and closes with a rule for living.
reading: Matthew 5 to 7 is the longest block of teaching in the Gospels. Matthew sets it on a mountain, so readers call it the Sermon on the *Mount*. Luke 6 has a shorter, similar sermon set on a plain. Many scholars think Matthew gathered sayings from different times into one speech. Christians have long read it as a summary of Jesus's teaching.

It opens with the *Beatitudes*, a set of blessings. Blessed are the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, those who hunger for what is right, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers. The pattern echoes the Psalms, which also begin with "blessed." Each line names a group that the world overlooks and says the kingdom belongs to them.

The middle of the sermon is a series of contrasts. "Ye have heard that it was said... but I say unto you." Jesus quotes a commandment and then presses it deeper. Do not kill becomes do not stay angry. Love your neighbor becomes love your enemies. Christians and scholars disagree about whether this replaces the Torah or intensifies it. Matthew 5:17 says Jesus came not to destroy the law but to fulfill it.

The sermon includes the Lord's Prayer and ends with the *golden rule*: treat others as you would want to be treated. The Jewish teacher Hillel, a generation earlier, is remembered in the Talmud as teaching a similar rule in a negative form. Comparing the two is a good way to see Jesus inside the Jewish teaching of his time.

words.d: the Sermon on the Mount is Matthew 5–7, Jesus's teaching gathered into one speech on a mountain
the blessings that open the Sermon on the Mount, each beginning "Blessed are"
treat others as you would want to be treated; Matthew 7:12 calls it the sum of the law and the prophets

look.title: The Golden Rule in Matthew
look.text: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
look.prompt: Jesus says this rule is "the law and the prophets." What do you think he means by summing up the whole Torah in one sentence?

check.q: Where in the Gospels is the Sermon on the Mount?
check.why: Matthew 5–7 holds the sermon; Luke 6 has a shorter parallel on a plain.

check.q: What are the Beatitudes?
choices: The blessings that open the sermon
check.why: Each Beatitude begins "Blessed are" and names a group the world overlooks.

check.q: Which earlier Jewish teacher is remembered for a rule like the golden rule?
check.why: The Talmud remembers Hillel teaching, in negative form, not to do to others what is hateful to you.

lessons.title: Miracle Stories
lessons.mainIdea: The Gospels tell of healings, feedings and stilled storms, and readers interpret these stories in different ways.
reading: A large share of Mark is made of *miracle* stories. Jesus heals a man with a withered hand, feeds a crowd with five loaves and two fish, and calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee. The Gospels use several words for these events. Mark and Matthew tend to say "works of power." John calls them *signs* and gives seven of them, each pointing to who Jesus is.

The stories share a shape. There is a need, an act or a word, and a response from the crowd. Mark 2 tells of a paralyzed man lowered through a roof by his friends. Jesus first says the man's sins are forgiven. Teachers of the law object. Then Jesus tells the man to rise and walk. The story is as much about the argument as about the healing.

Readers handle these stories in different ways. Many Christians believe the events happened as told. Some Christians read them as signs with a meaning beyond the event. Historians usually say they cannot judge whether a miracle occurred, but they can study what the stories meant to the people who told them. Jewish and Muslim readers have their own views; the Qur'an, for example, describes Jesus healing the sick by God's permission.

A public-school class does not decide whether a miracle happened. It can ask what each story says, what the people in it do and say, and how the story fits the Gospel it belongs to. That is reading, not believing or disbelieving.

words.d: in the Gospels, an act of healing, feeding or power over nature that shows God at work, as the writers present it
John's word for Jesus's miracles; John tells seven, each pointing to who Jesus is

look.title: Three Readers, One Story
look.text: Mark 4 tells of a storm on the Sea of Galilee. Jesus is asleep in the boat. The disciples wake him in fear. He speaks to the wind and sea, and there is a great calm. Then he asks why they are afraid. One reader says, this shows Jesus's power over nature. A second says, the point is the question about fear. A third says, a historian cannot test the weather, but can see that the story made the disciples look weak and Jesus strong.
look.prompt: Which reader is reading the text as scripture, which as literature, and which as history? Can one person do all three?

check.q: What word does John's Gospel use for Jesus's miracles?
check.why: John calls them signs and tells seven, each pointing to who Jesus is.

check.q: In Mark 2, what causes the argument with the teachers of the law?
choices: Jesus says the man's sins are forgiven
check.why: Before healing the paralyzed man, Jesus forgives his sins, and the teachers object; the healing follows the dispute.

check.q: How do historians usually treat miracle stories?
choices: They show each one did not happen
They study what the stories meant to those who told them
check.why: Historians say they cannot judge whether a miracle occurred, but they can study the stories' meaning and use.

lessons.title: The Passion Narrative
lessons.mainIdea: All four Gospels end with a long account of Jesus's last week, arrest, trial and death, called the Passion.
reading: The word *Passion* comes from a Latin word for suffering. It names the part of each Gospel that tells Jesus's last days in Jerusalem. All four Gospels give it more space than any other stretch of time. In Mark, the last week fills about a third of the book. Some scholars have called Mark a Passion story with a long introduction.

The outline is shared. Jesus enters Jerusalem before Passover. He shares a last meal with his disciples. He prays in a garden called Gethsemane. He is arrested at night, questioned by the high priest, and handed to Pilate. Pilate sentences him to *crucifixion*, a Roman punishment for rebels and slaves. He dies and is buried in a tomb.

The details differ. Mark and Matthew give one last saying from the cross, a line from Psalm 22. Luke gives three others. John gives three more. The Synoptics place the last supper as a Passover meal. John places the death on the day the Passover lambs were killed. Readers have worked hard to fit the accounts together. Many scholars prefer to read each on its own.

The Passion has a painful history. Some Christians over the centuries used it to blame Jewish people as a whole for Jesus's death. That reading fed violence against Jews. In 1965 the Catholic Church formally rejected it, and many Protestant churches have as well. A careful reader notes that the Gospels describe a Roman execution, ordered by a Roman governor, in a city of many opinions.

words.d: from Latin for suffering; the part of each Gospel that tells Jesus's arrest, trial and death
a Roman execution by being fixed to a wooden cross; used against rebels and slaves
the garden outside Jerusalem where the Gospels say Jesus prayed and was arrested

look.title: Two Timelines of One Week
look.text: Mark 14 says the last supper was the Passover meal, eaten the night before Jesus died. John 13 and 19 say Jesus died on the day of preparation, before the Passover meal was eaten, at the hour the lambs were killed. Both cannot be a simple calendar record. Some readers say John moved the date to make a point: Jesus dies as the Passover lamb. Others say Mark's timeline is the one with the symbolic shape.
look.prompt: What might each Gospel gain by placing the death where it does? Which kind of question is this, history or literature, or both?

check.q: What does "Passion" mean in Gospel study?
choices: The account of Jesus's suffering and death
check.why: Passion comes from the Latin for suffering and names the story of the last week, arrest, trial and death.

check.q: Who carried out crucifixion in the Gospels' world?
check.why: Crucifixion was a Roman punishment; the Gospels say Pilate, the governor, gave the sentence.

check.q: How does John's timing of the death differ from Mark's?
choices: John places it a year later
John places it before the Passover meal, when the lambs were killed
check.why: Mark's last supper is a Passover meal; John has Jesus die on the day of preparation.

lessons.title: The Resurrection Accounts
lessons.mainIdea: Each Gospel ends with an empty tomb and, as Christians believe, a risen Jesus, and each tells it differently.
reading: Every Gospel ends at a tomb. Women come early on the first day of the week. The stone is rolled away. The body is gone. From there the accounts differ. Mark's oldest manuscripts end at 16:8 with the women fleeing in fear, saying nothing. Matthew adds guards, an earthquake and a meeting in Galilee. Luke tells of two travelers on the road to Emmaus. John tells of Mary Magdalene in the garden and of Thomas, who doubts and then believes.

Christians believe that Jesus rose from the dead. This *resurrection* is the center of the Christian faith. Paul, writing before the Gospels, says in 1 Corinthians 15 that if Christ did not rise, faith is empty. Easter, the yearly Christian celebration of the resurrection, is the oldest Christian festival. Christians differ about how to picture it, but the belief unites them.

Readers outside the faith read the stories differently. Jewish tradition does not accept the resurrection. Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet, and most read the Qur'an as saying he was not killed on the cross. Historians note that the earliest followers plainly believed Jesus had appeared to them. Whether that belief was true is a question of faith, not history, and this course does not answer it.

What a class can do is read closely. Who comes to the tomb in each Gospel? Who speaks? Where do the followers meet Jesus, in Galilee or Jerusalem? Noting the differences is not an attack on the stories. Christian scholars have done it for centuries, and many see the differences as a sign that no one edited the accounts to match.

words.d: rising from the dead; Christians believe God raised Jesus on the third day after his death
the yearly Christian celebration of the resurrection; the oldest Christian festival
the village in Luke 24 where two travelers recognize the risen Jesus at a meal

look.title: How Mark's Oldest Copies End
look.text: And they went out quickly, and fled from the sepulchre; for they trembled and were amazed: neither said they any thing to any man; for they were afraid.
look.cite: Mark 16:8, King James Version (1611); the oldest manuscripts of Mark end here
look.prompt: If a book ends with frightened silence, what is the writer asking the reader to do? Why might later copyists have added a longer ending?

check.q: Where do the oldest manuscripts of Mark end?
choices: At 16:8, with the women afraid and silent
check.why: The oldest copies stop at Mark 16:8; the longer ending is found in later manuscripts.

check.q: Which Gospel tells of two travelers on the road to Emmaus?
check.why: Luke 24 tells the Emmaus story; John has Mary Magdalene and Thomas, Matthew a meeting in Galilee.

check.q: How does this course treat the question of whether the resurrection happened?
choices: It says the Gospels prove it
It says historians have disproved it
It says Jewish and Muslim readers accept it
It describes what each tradition believes and leaves the truth question to faith
check.why: The course attributes the belief to Christians, notes other traditions' views, and does not rule on the claim.

review.q: In Matthew 22, why was the question about paying tax to Caesar a trap?
choices: Because coins were not allowed in the Temple
Because either yes or no could get Jesus in trouble with a crowd or with Rome
Because Jesus did not know what a denarius was
Because the Pharisees wanted to pay more tax
review.why: Saying yes risked the crowd; saying no risked Rome; the question was built to catch him either way.

review.q: Which group was linked to the Temple priests and rejected resurrection?
review.why: The Gospels and Josephus describe the Sadducees as the priestly party that denied resurrection.

review.q: What is the usual range of dates scholars give for the four Gospels?
review.why: Most scholars place Mark c. 65–75, Matthew and Luke c. 80–90, and John c. 90–100 CE.

review.q: Why are Matthew, Mark and Luke called the Synoptic Gospels?
choices: They share many stories, order and wording
They were written by the same person
They all begin with a birth story
They were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls
review.why: Synoptic means "seen together"; the three share so much that they can be laid side by side.

review.q: In which chapters of Matthew is the Sermon on the Mount?
review.why: Matthew 5–7 holds the Beatitudes, the contrasts, the Lord's Prayer and the golden rule.

review.q: What do the Dead Sea Scrolls NOT contain?
review.why: The scrolls never mention Jesus or the early Christians; their value is the Jewish setting they reveal.

review.q: Who in Luke 10 stops to help the man left on the road?
review.why: The priest and Levite pass by; the Samaritan, from a distrusted group, shows mercy.

review.q: Which statement is written the way this course describes belief?
choices: Jesus rose from the dead on the third day.
Jesus did not rise from the dead.
Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead on the third day.
Everyone agrees that the tomb was empty.
review.why: The course attributes beliefs to those who hold them and does not assert or deny them.

chapters.title: Acts, Letters and Revelation
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a small group in Jerusalem become communities across the Roman world, and how did their writings become a book?

story.title: A Letter About a Brother
story.kicker: A prisoner writes to a man he knows well, about a slave who ran away and came back with a new name for himself.
paragraphs: Somewhere in the Roman Empire, in the 50s or 60s CE, a man sits in custody. He cannot travel, so he writes. His name is Paul, and he has a friend beside him named Onesimus. Onesimus is a slave. He has run away from his owner, a Christian named Philemon, who hosts a church in his house.

Under Roman law a runaway slave could be punished harshly. Paul knows this. He also knows Philemon. So he writes the shortest letter that carries his name, only 25 verses. He does not order Philemon to do anything. He says he could, but he would rather ask.

The letter is careful and warm. Paul calls Onesimus his child. He says he is sending him back, and that Philemon should receive him no longer as a slave, but as a beloved brother. He adds that if Onesimus owes anything, Paul will pay it. Then he asks Philemon to prepare a guest room.

The letter never says what Philemon did. Readers have argued about it ever since. Some say Paul was quietly undoing slavery from inside. Others say he left the system in place and only asked for kindness. In the 1800s, Americans on both sides of the slavery debate quoted this letter. It is one page long, and it has never stopped being read.

This chapter follows the story from Jerusalem to Rome. It reads Acts, the book that tells how the movement spread. It reads the letters of Paul and others as letters, with senders, receivers and reasons. It opens Revelation, the strange last book. And it asks how these writings, and not others, became the New Testament.
story.think: Paul says he could command Philemon but chooses to ask. What does a reader learn about the letter's purpose from that choice?

lessons.title: A Sequel to Luke
lessons.mainIdea: Acts continues the Gospel of Luke and tells how Jesus's followers spread from Jerusalem toward Rome.
reading: The Acts of the Apostles opens by looking back. Its first line speaks of a "former treatise," an earlier book, written to a man named Theophilus. The Gospel of Luke opens with the same name. Most scholars agree the two books share an author, whom tradition calls Luke. Together they make up about a quarter of the New Testament.

Acts has a shape. In its first chapter, the risen Jesus tells his followers they will be witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. The book then follows that map. Chapters 1 to 7 stay in Jerusalem. Chapters 8 to 12 move into Samaria and along the coast. Chapters 13 to 28 follow Paul across the sea to Greece and at last to Rome.

The word *apostle* means one who is sent. Acts uses it for the twelve closest followers of Jesus and, in places, for Paul. The people in Acts are Jews who believe Jesus is the *messiah*, the anointed one promised in the prophets. Over the course of the book, non-Jews, called Gentiles, join them. How Jews and Gentiles could share one table becomes the book's biggest question.

Historians read Acts with care. It was written decades after the events, and it tells the story with a purpose, as Luke's Gospel does. It also names real cities, officials and roads, many of them confirmed by inscriptions. Most scholars use it as a valuable source while checking it against Paul's own letters, which sometimes tell things differently.

words.d: "one who is sent"; the closest followers of Jesus, and Paul, as Acts and the letters use the word
the anointed one; Jews hoped for a king sent by God, and Christians believe Jesus is that messiah
a person who is not Jewish; in Acts, Gentiles begin to join the movement

look.title: The Map Acts Follows
look.text: But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
look.prompt: Trace how this one sentence lays out the whole book. Where does Acts actually end, and does that match "the uttermost part of the earth"?

check.q: Which Gospel does Acts continue?
check.why: Both Luke and Acts are addressed to Theophilus, and most scholars agree they share an author.

check.q: What does the word "apostle" mean?
check.why: Apostle comes from a Greek word for someone sent out; Acts uses it for the twelve and for Paul.

check.q: Where does the story of Acts end?
check.why: Acts 28 ends with Paul in Rome, following the map set out in Acts 1:8.

lessons.title: Pentecost, Peter and Stephen
lessons.mainIdea: The early chapters of Acts tell of a crowd at Pentecost, Peter's leadership and Stephen's death.
reading: Acts 2 opens at *Pentecost*, a Jewish harvest festival fifty days after Passover. Jews from many lands are in Jerusalem. The text says a sound like wind fills the house where the followers are gathered, and each begins to speak in a language others can understand. Peter stands and gives a speech. He quotes the prophet Joel and the Psalms. Acts says about three thousand people joined that day. Many Christians call this the birthday of the church.

*Peter*, a fisherman from Galilee, leads in these early chapters. He heals a man at the Temple gate. He is arrested and questioned by the council. Later, in Acts 10, he visits a Roman officer named Cornelius. Acts says a vision convinced Peter that Gentiles could join without first becoming Jews. That scene opens the door the rest of the book walks through.

Acts 6 and 7 tell of *Stephen*, chosen to help with the community's daily needs. He is accused of speaking against the Temple and the law. His long speech retells Israel's story from Abraham to Solomon. The council condemns him, and he is stoned. Acts calls him the first to die for the faith. A young man named Saul, the text notes, stood watching and approved.

These stories have been read in many ways. Christians see in them the pattern of witness and suffering. Jewish readers note that the disputes in Acts are arguments among Jews about the Temple, the law and the messiah. Historians see a small movement finding its shape. All three readings are possible from the same pages.

words.d: a Jewish festival fifty days after Passover; in Acts 2, the day the followers spoke in many languages
a fisherman from Galilee who leads the followers in the early chapters of Acts
a leader in Acts 6–7 whose speech and death Acts tells; Acts calls him the first to die for the faith

look.title: Two Festivals, One Day
look.text: In Jewish tradition Pentecost, called Shavuot, marks the giving of the Torah at Sinai and the wheat harvest. Acts 2 sets the followers' first public moment on that same day, with wind, fire and many languages. Jewish readers hear Sinai in the wind and fire, since Exodus 19 has both. Christian readers hear the beginning of the church. The text does not say which it intends.
look.prompt: What would Acts gain by choosing this festival for its scene? How might a Jewish and a Christian reader each hear the echo of Sinai?

check.q: What is Pentecost in Jewish tradition?
choices: A harvest festival fifty days after Passover
check.why: Pentecost, or Shavuot, comes fifty days after Passover and marks the harvest and, in tradition, the giving of the Torah.

check.q: What convinces Peter in Acts 10 that Gentiles may join?
choices: A vision before he visits Cornelius
check.why: Acts 10 tells of Peter's vision and his visit to the Roman officer Cornelius.

check.q: Who does Acts note was watching when Stephen was killed?
check.why: Acts 7 says a young man named Saul, later called Paul, stood by and approved.

lessons.title: Saul Becomes Paul
lessons.mainIdea: Acts tells three times how Saul, an opponent of the movement, became Paul, its most traveled messenger.
reading: Acts 9 tells of *Saul*, a Pharisee from Tarsus, on the road to Damascus. He is carrying letters that let him arrest followers of Jesus. The text says a light from heaven knocks him to the ground and a voice asks why he is persecuting it. Saul is blind for three days. A follower named Ananias lays hands on him, and his sight returns. Acts tells the story three times, in chapters 9, 22 and 26, each time a little differently.

Paul tells his own version in his letter to the Galatians. He says God revealed his Son to him, and that he did not consult anyone. He does not mention the road, the light or Ananias. Scholars compare the accounts and note that Acts and Paul agree on the main point: a sudden turn from opponent to messenger. Christians call this event Paul's *conversion*, though Paul himself never stopped being a Jew and said so.

The names can confuse readers. Saul was his Hebrew name. Paul was his Roman name. Acts 13 says he was called by both. He did not change his name at Damascus. As a citizen of Rome, a speaker of Greek and a student of the Torah, he could move between worlds. That is part of why the movement moved with him.

Jewish scholars have written about Paul too. Some see him as a Jew of his time working out how Gentiles fit into Israel's story. Others see him as the point where the two traditions began to part. This course notes both readings and does not choose between them.

words.d: Paul's Hebrew name; a Pharisee from Tarsus who, Acts says, first opposed the followers of Jesus
a sudden turn in belief or loyalty; the Christian name for what happened to Paul near Damascus

look.title: Acts and Paul Tell It
look.text: Acts 9 says a light from heaven struck Saul down on the road to Damascus, a voice spoke, and he was blind until Ananias prayed for him. Galatians 1, in Paul's own words, says God revealed his Son to him and that he went away to Arabia without consulting anyone. One is a story told by another writer; the other is a short line in a letter arguing a point.
look.prompt: Which account would a historian trust more, and why? What can the two agree on even though the details differ?

check.q: How many times does Acts tell the Damascus road story?
check.why: Acts 9, 22 and 26 each tell the story, with small differences.

check.q: Why did Paul have two names?
choices: Saul was his Hebrew name and Paul his Roman name
check.why: Acts 13 says he was called by both; the names reflect his Jewish and Roman worlds, not a change at conversion.

check.q: In which letter does Paul tell his own version of the event?
check.why: Galatians 1 gives Paul's own account; Acts is by another writer, and Revelation is not by Paul.

lessons.title: The Roads and the Sea
lessons.mainIdea: Acts traces Paul's travels across the eastern Mediterranean, using the roads and shipping lanes of the Roman Empire.
reading: Acts describes several long journeys. Paul's base is *Antioch* in Syria, a large city where Acts 11 says followers were first called Christians. From there he travels with companions like Barnabas, Silas and Timothy. Maps of the New Testament usually draw three missionary journeys and a final voyage to Rome. The numbering is a reader's tool; Acts itself does not count them.

The Roman Empire made such travel possible. Paved roads ran between major cities. Ships crossed the *Mediterranean* in the sailing season. Greek was spoken from Syria to Italy. Roman peace, the Pax Romana, kept most roads safe. Paul, a Roman citizen, could appeal to that system, and Acts shows him doing so more than once.

The journeys were still hard. In 2 Corinthians 11, Paul lists shipwrecks, beatings, hunger and nights without sleep. Acts 27 tells of a storm and a wreck on the island of Malta. Travel by land was slow, perhaps twenty miles a day on foot. A journey from Jerusalem to Rome could take months.

The pattern in each city repeats. Paul goes first to the synagogue, where he can argue from the scriptures. Some Jews and some Gentiles who worshiped with them join him. Others object. He moves on, leaving a small community behind. His letters, written later, go back to those communities.

words.d: a large city in Syria that was Paul's base; Acts 11 says followers were first called Christians there
the sea at the center of the Roman world; Paul's journeys crossed its eastern half
"Roman peace"; the long period of order and safe roads under the emperors

look.title: How Long Paul Stayed, as Acts Tells It
look.cite: Acts 18:11, 19:8–10 and 28:30, King James Version (1611); Ephesus combines three months and two years
look.prompt: Paul spent years in a few cities rather than weeks in many. What would that let him build that a quick visit could not?

check.q: Which city was Paul's base for his journeys?
check.why: Acts 13 sends Paul out from Antioch in Syria, and he returns there between journeys.

check.q: What made long-distance travel possible in Paul's world?
choices: Roman roads, shipping and a shared Greek language
A single language across the empire called Latin
check.why: Roman roads, sea lanes in the sailing season and common Greek let Paul move from Syria to Italy.

check.q: Where does Paul go first when he reaches a new city, according to Acts?
choices: The temple of the city's god
check.why: Acts repeats the pattern: Paul begins in the synagogue, where he can argue from the scriptures.

lessons.title: Five Cities
lessons.mainIdea: Philippi, Corinth, Ephesus and Rome each shaped a letter, and each still shows the traces of the ancient city.
reading: *Philippi* was a Roman colony in Macedonia, in northern Greece. Acts 16 says Paul's first convert there was Lydia, a merchant in purple cloth who hosted the new community. Paul and Silas were jailed there and freed, the text says, by an earthquake. Paul's later letter to the Philippians is his warmest, written from prison and full of thanks.

*Corinth* was a busy port city on the narrow strip of land joining northern and southern Greece. Acts 18 says Paul stayed eighteen months and worked as a tentmaker. His two long letters to the Corinthians answer questions and settle disputes in a community with many problems. An inscription naming Gallio, the official in Acts 18, helps date Paul's stay to about 51 or 52 CE.

*Ephesus* was a wealthy city in western Asia Minor, today Turkey, with a great temple of Artemis. Acts 19 tells of a riot led by silversmiths who sold shrines of the goddess. Paul stayed more than two years. Rome was the capital, and Paul wrote to its church before he had seen it. Acts ends with him there, under guard but teaching.

Chicago has a link to this map. The city's many congregations with Greek roots trace their faith to communities like these. And the names live on: Philippians, Corinthians, Ephesians and Romans are the titles of books that people in Chicago churches still hear read aloud each week.

words.d: a Roman colony in northern Greece where Acts 16 says Lydia hosted the first community
a Greek port city where Paul stayed eighteen months and to which he wrote two long letters
a rich city in Asia Minor with a temple of Artemis; Paul stayed there over two years

look.title: A Date From a Stone
look.text: Acts 18 says that while Paul was in Corinth, a Roman official named Gallio was proconsul of Achaia. In 1905 pieces of an inscription were found at Delphi in Greece. It mentions Gallio in that office, and its wording lets historians place his term at about 51 to 52 CE. Because Acts says Paul was in Corinth then, this stone is the firmest date in Paul's whole life.
look.prompt: Why is a stone that never mentions Paul so useful for dating him? What does it show about how historians use the New Testament?

check.q: Who hosted the first community at Philippi, according to Acts 16?
check.why: Acts 16 names Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, as Paul's first convert there and the host of the group.

check.q: Why does the Gallio inscription matter?
choices: It names Paul as a tentmaker
It records the earthquake at Philippi
It lists the books of the New Testament
It helps date Paul's stay in Corinth to c. 51–52 CE
check.why: Acts 18 places Paul in Corinth under Gallio; the Delphi inscription dates Gallio's term.

check.q: What caused the riot at Ephesus in Acts 19?
choices: Silversmiths who sold shrines of Artemis
check.why: Acts 19 says silversmiths feared losing business as the new movement grew.

lessons.title: How an Ancient Letter Works
lessons.mainIdea: Paul's letters follow the shape of ordinary Greek letters, with a greeting, a thanksgiving, a body and a farewell.
reading: Thousands of ordinary letters from the Roman world survive on papyrus. They open with the sender's name, then the receiver's, then a greeting. Then comes the business, then a farewell. Paul's letters use the same shape and stretch it. His greetings are long and his thanksgivings can run a whole chapter. Scholars call this form the *epistle*.

Look at the opening of Romans. Paul names himself first, in a sentence that runs six verses. He names the receivers: all in Rome who are loved by God. Then comes his greeting. It replaces the usual Greek word for "hello" with two words that matter to him: *grace* and peace. Nearly every letter of his begins this way.

After the greeting comes a thanksgiving for the readers, then the body. The body is where Paul teaches, argues and answers questions. Near the end comes a section of practical advice. Then a farewell with greetings to named people. Romans 16 greets more than two dozen by name, including women like Phoebe, Priscilla and Junia.

Knowing the form helps a reader. A letter is one side of a conversation. Paul writes to a real community with a real problem. When he says "you," he means them, not every reader since. Understanding the *occasion*, the situation that caused the letter, is the first step in reading one.

words.d: a letter, especially a formal one; the New Testament letters are often called epistles
God's free favor, in Paul's letters; his greetings replace the usual Greek "hello" with "grace and peace"
the situation that caused a letter to be written; the first thing to work out when reading one

look.title: Two Openings
look.text: An ordinary papyrus letter from Roman Egypt: 'Apion to Epimachus his father and lord, many greetings. Before all things I pray that you are in health.' Romans 1, in short: 'Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle... To all that be in Rome, beloved of God... Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.'
look.prompt: Mark the sender, receiver and greeting in each. What has Paul kept from the ordinary form, and what has he added or changed?

check.q: What is the usual order of parts in Paul's letters?
check.why: Paul follows the Greek letter form: sender and receiver with a greeting, thanks, the body, then a farewell.

check.q: What two words replace the ordinary Greek "hello" in Paul's greetings?
check.why: Paul's greetings say "grace to you and peace," turning a common word into a blessing.

check.q: What does "occasion" mean in reading a letter?
choices: The festival on which it was read
The city where it was copied
The situation that caused it to be written
check.why: Each letter answers a real situation in a real community; finding it is the first step in reading.

lessons.title: Paul's Letters in Order
lessons.mainIdea: Thirteen letters carry Paul's name; the Bible orders them by length, and scholars debate which he wrote himself.
reading: Thirteen New Testament letters open with Paul's name. In the Bible they run from Romans to Philemon. That order is not the order they were written. It is roughly by length, longest first, with letters to churches before letters to persons. So Romans, the longest, comes first, and Philemon, the shortest, comes last.

Scholars ask which letters Paul wrote himself. Most agree on seven: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. These are called the *undisputed* letters. About the other six, scholars disagree. Some think followers wrote in Paul's name after his death, a common practice in the ancient world. Others think Paul wrote them all. Christians hold both views.

In the order of writing, 1 Thessalonians is usually put first, around 50 CE. That makes it the oldest book in the New Testament, older than any Gospel. Galatians and the Corinthian letters follow in the 50s. Romans, often called his most complete statement, is dated about 57 CE. Philippians and Philemon were written from prison, though scholars debate which prison.

Each letter has a subject. Galatians argues that Gentiles need not keep the whole Torah. 1 Corinthians answers a list of questions and includes the famous chapter on love. Romans lays out Paul's whole way of thinking about *faith*, law and God's promises to Israel. Reading a letter as a whole, from greeting to farewell, keeps each idea in its place.

words.d: the seven letters nearly all scholars agree Paul wrote himself: Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon
trust in God; a key word in Paul's letters, especially Romans and Galatians
1 Thessalonians, a letter usually dated c. 50 CE and thought to be the oldest book in the New Testament

look.title: The End of the Love Chapter
look.text: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
look.prompt: The King James Bible uses "charity" where most modern translations say "love." What does each English word suggest, and why might a translator choose one over the other?

check.q: How are Paul's letters ordered in the New Testament?
choices: By the date they were written
By the size of the city
check.why: Romans, the longest, comes first and Philemon, the shortest, last; churches come before persons.

check.q: Which letter is usually called the oldest book in the New Testament?
check.why: 1 Thessalonians is dated c. 50 CE, before any Gospel; Mark is usually placed c. 70 CE.

check.q: What does "undisputed" mean about seven of Paul's letters?
choices: They are the only ones in the canon
They were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls
Nearly all scholars agree Paul wrote them himself
check.why: Scholars debate the other six; the seven undisputed letters are accepted as Paul's own by almost everyone.

lessons.title: Philemon and the Catholic Letters
lessons.mainIdea: Philemon shows a letter at work in one household, and seven "catholic" letters speak to the church at large.
reading: Philemon is one page long and shows how a letter can work. Paul writes to a friend about a slave, Onesimus, who has come to Paul and, the letter says, become a believer. Paul sends him back. He asks Philemon to receive him as a brother. He offers to pay any debt. He also says, in a gentle way, that Philemon owes Paul his very self.

The letter leaves the big question open. Does "brother" mean Onesimus should be freed? Paul does not say. Some readers say the whole letter points that way. Others note that neither Paul nor any New Testament writer calls for the end of *slavery* as a system. In the 1800s both sides in the American debate quoted him. Frederick Douglass and others rejected readings that used Paul to defend slavery. A careful reader states what the text says and what it leaves unsaid.

After Paul's letters come seven others, named for their writers rather than their readers: James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John, and Jude. They are called the *catholic* letters, from a Greek word meaning general or universal, because most are addressed to the church at large rather than one city. The word here has nothing to do with the Roman Catholic Church as a name.

James is practical and reads almost like Proverbs. It says faith without works is dead, a line Christians have debated beside Paul's words about faith. 1 Peter writes to scattered communities facing hostility. 1 John returns again and again to love. A letter called Hebrews, placed after Philemon, names no author. It reads more like a sermon than a letter.

words.d: owning people as property; common in the Roman world and never abolished by any New Testament writer, though readers have argued about Philemon
from a Greek word for general or universal; the seven letters James through Jude, addressed to the church at large
a New Testament book placed after Philemon that names no author and reads like a sermon

lessons.title: Revelation: Visions Under Rome
lessons.mainIdea: Revelation is an apocalypse, a book of visions and symbols written to encourage churches under Roman pressure.
reading: The last book of the New Testament opens with a man named John on *Patmos*, a small island off the coast of Asia Minor. He says he is there because of the word of God. He writes to seven churches in nearby cities, including Ephesus. Then he describes visions: a throne, a scroll with seven seals, a dragon, beasts, a woman clothed with the sun, and at last a new heaven and a new earth.

Revelation belongs to a genre called *apocalypse*, from a Greek word meaning unveiling. Daniel in the Hebrew Bible is the same kind of book. An apocalypse uses symbols, numbers and visions to speak to people in a hard time. Seven means completeness. A beast stands for an empire. Babylon, the city that destroyed the first Temple, stands in Revelation for Rome.

Most scholars date the book to about 95 CE, in the last years of the emperor *Domitian*. A second-century writer, Irenaeus, gives that date. Some argue for an earlier date under Nero. Either way, the churches faced pressure to honor the emperor as divine, and some had suffered. The book tells them to hold on, and it promises that Rome will fall and God will make all things new.

Christians have read Revelation in very different ways. Some read it as a map of the future. Others read it as a message for its own time that still speaks. Others read it as poetry of hope. Eastern Orthodox churches long left it out of their public readings. It is the only New Testament book that some early church lists were unsure about.

words.d: a small island off Asia Minor where Revelation says its writer, John, received his visions
"unveiling"; a kind of writing that uses visions and symbols to speak hope to people in a hard time
Roman emperor 81–96 CE, in whose last years most scholars date Revelation

lessons.title: How 27 Books Became One
lessons.mainIdea: The New Testament canon formed over three centuries, and Athanasius's list of 367 CE is the first to match today's 27 books.
reading: No one sat down in the first century and wrote the New Testament. Gospels and letters circulated one by one. Communities copied the ones they valued and read them aloud. Over time some writings were accepted almost everywhere: the four Gospels, Acts and Paul's letters. Others were debated: Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation. Still others, like the Shepherd of Hermas, were read for a while and then set aside.

The list of accepted books is called the *canon*, from a Greek word for a measuring rod. Several forces shaped it. Around 140 CE a teacher named Marcion proposed a short canon with one Gospel and ten letters of Paul, and rejected the Hebrew Bible. Most churches rejected his list, and in doing so began to state their own. A fragment from around 200 CE, called the Muratorian fragment, gives an early list close to today's.

The first surviving list with exactly the 27 books of today's New Testament comes from *Athanasius*, bishop of Alexandria, in an Easter letter of 367 CE. Councils in North Africa in the 390s agreed. The order and the number have been stable since, though churches still differ on the Old Testament. The word "Bible" itself means "the books," plural.

Christians explain the canon in different ways. Some say the church recognized the books God had inspired. Others describe a human process guided by use, tradition and argument. Historians describe the process without ruling on the first claim. A class can trace how the list took shape and leave the question of why to each reader.

words.d: from a Greek word for measuring rod; the list of books a tradition accepts as scripture
bishop of Alexandria whose Easter letter of 367 CE is the first surviving list of exactly today's 27 New Testament books
a teacher of c. 140 CE who proposed a short canon and rejected the Hebrew Bible; most churches rejected his list
